summary: A Python Morsels screencast by Trey Hunner explaining how square-bracket subscript notation works on objects through the __getitem__ method, covering both list indexing and dictionary key lookups. It demonstrates a ForgivingIndexer class that converts string and float indexes to integers, and notes that implementing __getitem__ is how sequence-like and mapping-like objects support square brackets. It is part of the Dunder Methods series.
one_line: Explains how implementing __getitem__ lets custom Python objects support square-bracket index and key lookups.
key_facts: Python lists support indexing with square brackets, e.g. colors[1] returns 'blue' from ["purple", "blue", "green", "pink"].
Python dictionaries support key lookups with square brackets, e.g. fruit_counts["pear"] returns 2.
Subscript notation with square brackets is powered by the __getitem__ method.
Any object implementing a __getitem__ method can be used with subscript notation.
The ForgivingIndexer class defines __init__ to store a sequence and __getitem__ that returns self.sequence[int(index)].
ForgivingIndexer converts the string "2" to an integer, so colors["2"] returns 'green'.
ForgivingIndexer converts the float 3.2 to an integer, so colors[3.2] returns 'pink'.
You most often implement __getitem__ in list-like objects (sequences) or dictionary-like objects (mappings).
The screencast is 1 minute 25 seconds long and is part of the Dunder Methods series.
The article is written by Trey Hunner, published Jan. 31, 2022, and applies to Python 3.8 through 3.12.
The series description states that overloading operators, protocols, and functionality is done by implementing dunder methods.
The next video in the series is 'Making the len function work on your Python objects', which requires a __len__ method.
